title: Jeremiah 42:7–22
context: After ten days the LORD answers through Jeremiah. If the remnant stays in the land, the LORD will build and plant them, for he grieves over the distress he has brought, and he will protect them from the king of Babylon. If they insist on going to Egypt for safety, the sword and famine they fear will overtake them there. Jeremiah warns that they have dealt deceitfully by asking for guidance they did not intend to follow. Both traditions read the passage as shared ground about God’s conditional mercy and the seriousness of disobedience.

verses.text: After ten days, the LORD’s word came to Jeremiah.
verses.arminianNotes:
After ten days the LORD’s word comes to Jeremiah. The answer is not immediate.

Arminian readers see the prophet waiting on God rather than giving his own opinion, even under pressure from an anxious community.
verses.reformedNotes:
The delay underlines that the answer is the LORD’s, not Jeremiah’s calculation.

Reformed readers see God answering in his own time. Both traditions read this as shared ground about patient waiting on God’s word before acting, and about the integrity of true prophecy.

verses.text: Then he called Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces who were with him, and all the people from the least even to the greatest,
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah calls Johanan, the captains, and all the people, least to greatest. Everyone must hear.

Arminian readers see the whole community addressed, since all had joined in the request and the oath, and all must now decide.
verses.reformedNotes:
The repeated phrase “from the least even to the greatest” echoes 42:1.

Reformed readers see God’s word addressed to the whole people. Both traditions read this as shared ground and note that the answer is given publicly, so that no one can claim not to have heard it.

verses.text: and said to them, “The LORD, the God of Israel, to whom you sent me to present your supplication before him, says:
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah introduces the answer from the LORD, the God of Israel, to whom they sent him with their plea. The message carries God’s authority.

Arminian readers see the prophet faithfully delivering what he received, without softening it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah reminds them that they themselves initiated this inquiry.

Reformed readers see the authority of God’s word framed by the people’s own request. Both traditions read this as shared ground about receiving God’s answer once it has been sought, which the people had sworn to obey.

verses.text: ‘If you will still live in this land, then I will build you, and not pull you down, and I will plant you, and not pluck you up; for I grieve over the distress that I have brought on you.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD promises that if they stay, he will build and plant them, not pull down or pluck up, “for I grieve over the distress that I have brought on you.” Mercy is offered.

Arminian readers see a real conditional offer.
verses.reformedNotes:
The language of building and planting recalls 1:10 and 24:6. On divine grief and relenting, see the boxes at 1 Samuel 15:29 and Jonah 3:10.

Reformed readers see mercy within God’s purpose. Both traditions read this as shared ground.

verses.text: Don’t be afraid of the king of Babylon, of whom you are afraid. Don’t be afraid of him,’ says the LORD, ‘for I am with you to save you, and to deliver you from his hand.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD tells them not to fear the king of Babylon, for he is with them to save and deliver them. Fear is answered by promise.

Arminian readers see trust in God offered as the alternative to flight driven by fear.
verses.reformedNotes:
Fear of Babylon is the motive the narrative gives for the plan to flee (41:18).

Reformed readers see God’s presence as the ground of courage. Both traditions read this as clear shared ground about trusting God’s promise rather than acting from fear.

verses.text: I will grant you mercy, that he may have mercy on you, and cause you to return to your own land.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will show them mercy so that the king will have mercy and let them return to their land. God works through a foreign king.

Arminian readers see God’s gracious provision offered to those who will trust and stay.
verses.reformedNotes:
The promise assumes that God can move the heart of Babylon’s king toward mercy.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty over rulers serving his people’s good. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God’s mercy reaching his people even through those who had conquered them.

verses.text: “ ‘But if you say, “We will not dwell in this land,” so that you don’t obey the LORD your God’s voice,
verses.arminianNotes:
But if they say they will not stay, and so disobey the LORD’s voice, the alternative follows. The choice is laid out.

Arminian readers see a genuine either-or set before the people, with real consequences for each path.
verses.reformedNotes:
The conditional form mirrors covenant choices elsewhere in Scripture.

Reformed readers see God’s word calling for obedience. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the seriousness of choosing between obedience and disobedience when God has spoken clearly.

verses.text: saying, “No, but we will go into the land of Egypt, where we will see no war, nor hear the sound of the trumpet, nor have hunger of bread; and there we will dwell;” ’
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD anticipates their reasoning: in Egypt they will see no war, hear no trumpet, and lack no bread. Egypt promises security.

Arminian readers see a natural human desire for safety tempting them away from trust.
verses.reformedNotes:
The hopes are understandable after war and famine, and the text reports them plainly.

Reformed readers see the attraction of human security over God’s word. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the pull of apparent safety, without mocking the people’s fears.

verses.text: now therefore hear the LORD’s word, O remnant of Judah! The LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says, ‘If you indeed set your faces to enter into Egypt, and go to live there,
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD calls the remnant of Judah to hear: if they are set on going to Egypt to live there, consequences will follow. The warning begins.

Arminian readers see God warning in advance so that the choice may still be reconsidered.
verses.reformedNotes:
The phrase ‘set your faces’ suggests firm determination.

Reformed readers see God’s warning as an act of mercy. Both traditions read this as shared ground about God speaking clearly before judgment falls, so that the people know the stakes of their decision.

verses.text: then it will happen that the sword, which you fear, will overtake you there in the land of Egypt; and the famine, about which you are afraid, will follow close behind you there in Egypt; and you will die there.
verses.arminianNotes:
The sword they fear will overtake them in Egypt, and the famine they dread will follow them there, and they will die. What they flee will find them.

Arminian readers see the irony of a choice that brings the very outcome it sought to avoid.
verses.reformedNotes:
The verse turns their hopes in verse 14 upside down.

Reformed readers see that no place is beyond God’s reach. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the futility of seeking safety in disobedience.

verses.text: So will it be with all the men who set their faces to go into Egypt to live there. They will die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence. None of them will remain or escape from the evil that I will bring on them.’
verses.arminianNotes:
All who set their faces to go to Egypt will die by sword, famine, and pestilence; none will escape. The warning is comprehensive.

Arminian readers see the gravity of the decision in front of them, which is still open at this point in the narrative.
verses.reformedNotes:
The familiar triad of sword, famine, and pestilence recurs throughout Jeremiah.

Reformed readers see God’s word certain to be fulfilled. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the seriousness of the warning and do not soften it.

verses.text: For the LORD of Armies, the God of Israel, says: ‘As my anger and my wrath has been poured out on the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so my wrath will be poured out on you, when you enter into Egypt; and you will be an object of horror, an astonishment, a curse, and a reproach; and you will see this place no more.’
verses.arminianNotes:
As God’s wrath fell on Jerusalem, so it will fall on them in Egypt; they will become a horror and reproach and never see this place again. Judgment follows them.

Arminian readers see consequences tied to their choice.
verses.reformedNotes:
The comparison with Jerusalem’s fall makes the warning concrete.

Reformed readers see the consistency of God’s justice. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the continuity between judgment on Jerusalem and judgment on those who repeat its disobedience.

verses.text: “The LORD has spoken concerning you, remnant of Judah, ‘Don’t go into Egypt!’ Know certainly that I have testified to you today.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah declares that the LORD has said, “Don’t go into Egypt!” and that he has testified to them today. The command is plain.

Arminian readers see a clear word that leaves the people fully responsible for their response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah seems to sense their resistance before they speak.

Reformed readers see God’s word plainly given. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the clarity of God’s command and the responsibility of those who have heard it.

verses.text: For you have dealt deceitfully against your own souls; for you sent me to the LORD your God, saying, ‘Pray for us to the LORD our God; and according to all that the LORD our God says, so declare to us, and we will do it.’
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah says they have dealt deceitfully against their own souls, for they sent him to pray and promised to do whatever God said. Their oath returns.

Arminian readers see self-deception in a request never meant to be obeyed if unwelcome.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah’s charge recalls their promise in 42:5–6.

Reformed readers see the deceitfulness of the heart. Both traditions read this as shared ground about honesty before God and the danger of seeking guidance only to confirm a decision already made.

verses.text: I have declared it to you today; but you have not obeyed the LORD your God’s voice in anything for which he has sent me to you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah says he has declared God’s word, but they have not obeyed in anything. Their disobedience is named.

Arminian readers see a free refusal of God’s guidance after it was requested and promised to be followed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Jeremiah speaks as though their decision is already evident, though chapter 43 narrates it.

Reformed readers see human resistance to God’s revealed will. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the gap between asking for guidance and obeying it.

verses.text: Now therefore know certainly that you will die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence in the place where you desire to go to live.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah concludes that they will die by sword, famine, and pestilence in the place where they wish to live. The warning ends starkly.

Arminian readers see consequences flowing from their chosen path.
verses.reformedNotes:
The closing words repeat the warning of verse 17 and anticipate chapter 44.

Reformed readers see God’s word sure to stand. Both traditions read this as shared ground about the seriousness of rejecting God’s clear guidance, reported soberly without elaboration on the suffering to come.
